2017_116_121917mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of December 19, 2017 at the Services Building — the meeting that committed the district to building an Early Childhood Center, and moved it. Item 8.E authorizes construction documents and bidding, relocates the project from Section 16 to the vacant land at the Niles Continuing Education site, creates an Early Childhood Center Fund, transfers $4,700,000 into it from Capital Maintenance, restricts all property-sale revenue through June 30, 2020 to it, and appoints Barton Malow construction manager of record. It also awards $1,498,090.00 of roofing and $82,700.00 of asbestos abatement, extends the TESA contract to June 30, 2021, amends the General Fund to $148,584,440, and endorses the Michigan School Finance Research Collaborative.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, December 19, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
A Mission Moment on Wass Elementary's Armed Forces Student Lesson.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the November 14 workshop, the November 21 meeting and the November 28 special workshop, the October 2017 Treasurer's Report, and a resolution supporting the School Finance Research Collaborative. The November 14 workshop covered Diversity & Inclusion Part II with Dr. Jay Marks and previewed the bus purchase and PowerSchool contract.

**Treasurer's Report — October 2017**
Total check disbursements are $9,022,755.09, the General Fund group $4,685,631.59 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,313,774.74. Adding $2,010,787.36 of wire transfers, $211,824.56 of P-Card purchases and $16,774.75 of ACH debits, less $1,538.88 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,260,602.88.

**The School Finance Research Collaborative**
The item opens with a question and a blunt answer: "A very important question commonly asked among Michigan's public school leaders is 'How much does it cost to educate a child?' The answer is simple and straightforward — **we don't know.** The state of Michigan has never had a comprehensive school adequacy study conducted." Education experts and business leaders have formed the broad-based, bipartisan Collaborative; MASA and MASB support it and local boards are asked to endorse.

The resolution's recitals: Michigan ranks **32nd in student achievement nationwide**; the Governor's 21st Century Education Commission found "the urgency could not be greater regarding the falling K-12 performance," with Michiganders ranking **41st on fourth-grade reading**; efficient distribution requires a transparent calculation of what it costs to meet performance standards, and students with greater educational needs should receive additional resources to have an equal chance. It notes the 2016 statewide Adequacy Study produced valuable information but **used only one methodology** and did not fully examine special education costs, preschool, charter schools, career and technical education, the impact of high concentrations of special needs students, or geographically isolated and very small districts.

**Personnel**
The **Troy Educational Secretaries Association (TESA)**, MEA/NEA contract is extended **through June 30, 2021** — a two-year extension. This is the contract whose negotiation had taken the Board into closed session on December 5. (A month later the Board would extend TESPA, the support personnel association, through June 30, 2022 on the same pattern.)

**Business — roofing and abatement**
Roof replacement at five district buildings, reviewed by district roofing consultant WeatherTech with Michelle Kerns and Rob Carson: **J. D. Chandler $888,400.00, Royal West $473,500.00, 10% contingency $136,190.00 — $1,498,090.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

Asbestos abatement at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard, reviewed by Rob Carson, awarded to **NOVA Environmental, Inc. in the amount of "$82,700.00.00"** as printed. Both the contractor and the amount are defective: NOVA is the district's abatement *consultant*, not the abatement contractor, and the figure carries a doubled decimal. The Board would adopt a corrected resolution on January 16, 2018 substituting **Qualified Abatement** at $82,700.00, with President Schmidt explaining that "the name of the consulting firm was inadvertently put in the initial resolution."

**Business — the budget amendment**
General Fund Budget Amendment #1 for 2017-18 sets the fund at **$148,584,440**.

**Business 8.E — the Early Childhood Center**
The district "has been engaged in the process of designing an Early Childhood Center since August of 2016." The recitals restate the mission, the vision of becoming a World Class educational entity by 2020, and that **one of the four established pillars is Investing in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten students**; they recount the March 21, 2017 resolution appointing TMP Architecture at not more than $933,716 for phases 1 through 4, and note a comprehensive and collaborative design process involving many stakeholders since March 2017.

Seven resolved clauses:

1. Authorize **continued design development, preparation of construction documents, and bidding**.
2. Develop the center **on the vacant land located on the current Niles Continuing Education site**.
3. Authorize administration to **establish an Early Childhood Center Fund**.
4. Transfer **$4,700,000 from the Capital Maintenance Fund** into it, restricted to the project.
5. Direct that **revenue from any property sale between this resolution and June 30, 2020** be deposited into the fund and restricted to the project.
6. Appoint **Barton Malow Company** construction manager of record, consistent with its bond-work proposal, paid from the ECC Fund professional services budget.
7. **Supersede and replace any and all previous conflicting resolutions.**

Clause 2 is the substantive change. The March 2017 resolution had sited the center on "approximately 8 acres of Section 16" while preserving the balance; here the project moves to the Niles site — which is why Section 16 could later be sold whole, and why the preschool was built at 205 Square Lake Road. Clause 7 is what makes that stick. Clause 5 broadens the March rule: no longer only the three named parcels, but *any* property sale for two and a half years.

**Other**
Adoption of MASB's Board of Education Governance Standards, "intended to help support school boards in their efforts to govern responsibly and effectively on behalf of all students."

The agenda index places the Mission Moment heading under item 7 Curriculum through a layout error; it belongs to item 2.

**Recognition 2.A.** A TSD Mission Moment on Wass Elementary School's Armed Forces Student Lesson.

**Consent minutes: the November 14, 2017 workshop.** President Philippart called the workshop to order at 6:03 p.m. with Mr. Schmidt absent. Present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Carson, Griffor, Harris, Soggs and West, plus three members of the audience. The agenda was public communication; board professional learning on Diversity & Inclusion, Part II with Dr. Jay Marks, Diversity & Equity Consultant; and a business services update covering the bus purchase discussion and the PowerSchool contract — both of which the Board acted on at the November 21 meeting the following week.

**Treasurer's Report, October 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $4,313,774.74, with Total General Fund of $4,685,631.59 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $9,022,755.09. Adding ACH debits of $16,774.75, outgoing wire transfers of $2,010,787.36 and P-Card purchases of $211,824.56, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $1,538.88, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,260,602.88. The middle sections of the packet are the October check register run by fund.

**Consent item 5.E: School Finance Research Collaborative.** The item begins with a question and an unusually direct answer: "A very important question commonly asked among Michigan's public school leaders is 'How much does it cost to educate a child?' The answer is simple and straightforward - we don't know. The state of Michigan has never had a comprehensive school adequacy study conducted, which is why education experts and business leaders from all over the state have formed the broad-based, bipartisan Michigan School Finance Research Collaborative. This group believes that it's time to change the way Michigan's schools are funded to ensure that every student gets the education needed to reach his or her full potential."

MASA and MASB support the Collaborative's work and would like to send a clear message to policymakers in Lansing that the work is critical if Michigan's public schools and the services they provide are going to be funded in the most effective and appropriate manner possible. Local school boards are asked to consider adopting a resolution in support of the Collaborative and the work it is doing to determine the true cost of educating Michigan's public school students.

The resolution's recitals build the case. The Michigan Constitution states that the legislature shall maintain and support a system of free public elementary and secondary schools as defined by law. Michigan ranks 32nd in student achievement nationwide according to recent research. The Governor's 21st Century Education Commission states that the urgency could not be greater regarding falling K-12 performance, further stating that Michiganders underperform their peers, ranking 41st on fourth-grade reading performance nationally. The Commission further stated that Michigan needs to efficiently distribute resources, that efficient distribution requires a transparent calculation of what it costs to meet performance standards, and that students with greater educational needs should be provided with additional resources where needed to have an equal chance of meeting those standards.

A further recital addresses the study the state did conduct: in 2016 the State of Michigan conducted a comprehensive statewide cost study, an Adequacy Study, that produced and provided valuable information but used only one methodology and did not fully examine special education costs due to data availability issues, did not examine preschool, charter schools, career and technical education, the impact of high concentrations of special needs students, or the cost challenges faced by geographically isolated schools and very small school districts. The recitals conclude that the way Michigan's public schools are funded is fundamentally in need of examination.

The item sits interestingly beside the rest of the packet. The same Board that here endorses a statewide finding that nobody knows what educating a child costs is, on the same agenda, transferring $4,700,000 of its own accumulated funds into a preschool it decided to build with money from selling land — an object lesson in a district financing what the state formula does not.

**Personnel 6.A: extension of the TESA contract.** The Board is recommended to approve the extension of the Troy Educational Secretaries Association (TESA), MEA/NEA contract through June 30, 2021 — an extension of two years to the current TESA Collective Bargaining Agreement. The resolution so approves, and the collective bargaining agreement between the Troy School District and the Troy Educational Secretaries Association/MEA/NEA is attached in full.

The attached agreement covers the ordinary ground of a support-staff contract: work performed within the TESA/MEA/NEA unit and the amount of supervision necessary; reporting lines to the immediate supervisor and to the TESA/MEA/NEA president; mileage when employees must use a personal vehicle; seniority dated from the most recent date of hire for a TESA/MEA/NEA position; and provisions applying specifically to employees hired into a TESA bargaining unit position after June 30, 2011.

The timing connects to the January 2018 packet: the December 5, 2017 closed session, whose minutes appear in the February 2018 packet, was held to discuss the TESA contract extension, and the January 9, 2018 closed session was held on TESPA — the Board extending its two support-staff agreements in successive months, TESA to June 30, 2021 and TESPA to June 30, 2022.

**Business 8.A: 2017-18 budget amendment resolution.** The Budget Amendment Resolution for fiscal year 2017-18 covers the General Fund. The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes, and the resolution amends and approves the general appropriations and budget for the General Fund as attached and made part of the official minutes of the December 19, 2017 regular meeting. The amended General Fund total is $148,584,440. This is General Fund Budget Amendment #1 for the year; Amendment 2 would follow in April 2018.

**Business 8.B: roofing bid.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on roof replacement work at five district buildings. Bid responses were reviewed by WeatherTech, the district's roofing consultant, along with Michelle Kerns and Rob Carson. The resolution awards the roof replacement as follows, approved as expenditures of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund: J. D. Chandler $888,400.00; Royal West $473,500.00; and a 10% contingency of $136,190.00, for a total of $1,498,090.00.

The same two contractors had split the district's December 2016 roofing award, also with a 10% contingency, with their relative shares reversed this time.

**Business 8.C: asbestos abatement.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on asbestos abatement work at Costello, Martell, Morse and Leonard Elementary Schools, with bids reviewed by Mr. Rob Carson, Director of Operations. The resolution awards the bid for asbestos abatement at those four schools to NOVA Environmental, Inc. in the amount of "$82,700.00.00" and approves that amount as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

Both the contractor name and the figure are defective as printed. The amount carries a doubled decimal — "$82,700.00.00" — and NOVA Environmental is the district's asbestos *consultant*, the firm that prepares contractor award recommendations, not the abatement contractor. The error was caught within weeks: the January 16, 2018 packet carries a corrected resolution awarding the same work at the same four schools to **Qualified Abatement** at $82,700.00, reproducing this original with the contractor name struck through and the correct name substituted. The January 16 minutes record President Schmidt explaining to the Board that the corrected resolution "was just an error naming the company that was awarded the bid" and that "the name of the consulting firm was inadvertently put in the initial resolution," with the December 19 minutes also amended to reflect the correction.

The abatement is the companion to the mechanical and electrical work at the same four elementary schools awarded a month earlier under Bid Pack 21 — floor tile and insulation have to come out before mechanical systems go in.

**Business 8.D and 8.E: the Early Childhood Center.** Item 8.D is a report; 8.E is the resolution, and it is the most consequential item in the 2017 packets.

The item records that the district "has been engaged in the process of designing an Early Childhood Center since August of 2016" — placing the origin four months before the December 2016 workshop at which an "Early Childhood Timeline" first appears in these packets, and seven months before the March 2017 resolution that appointed the architect.

The recitals restate the framework: the Board's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; its vision is to become a World Class educational entity by 2020; one of the four established pillars in becoming World Class by 2020 is Investing in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten students; the district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center to service its pre-kindergarten students; the Board as part of a resolution approved on March 21, 2017 appointed TMP Architecture as architect of record and authorized it to commence the design process in accordance with its proposal dated March 10, 2017, at a cost not to exceed $933,716 to complete phases 1 through 4, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund; and the district has been engaged in a comprehensive and collaborative design process involving many stakeholders since March 2017.

The seven resolved clauses are:

1. The School District authorizes the continued design development, preparation of construction documents, and bidding of an Early Childhood Center.
2. The School District desires to develop the Early Childhood Center on the vacant land located on the current Niles Continuing Education site.
3. The School District authorizes Administration to establish an Early Childhood Center Fund.
4. The School District authorizes a transfer of $4,700,000 from the Capital Maintenance Fund into the Early Childhood Center Fund and the funds be restricted for the development of the Early Childhood Center.
5. The School District directs revenue generated from any sale of property between the date of this resolution through June 30, 2020 be deposited into the Early Childhood Fund and restricted for use in the development of the Early Childhood Center.
6. The School District appoints Barton Malow Company as the Construction Manager of Record and authorizes Administration to finalize a contract with Barton Malow consistent with their proposal submitted for the bond work, with their services approved as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund Professional Services Budget.
7. This resolution supersedes and replaces any and all previous resolutions in whole or in part that conflict with this resolution.

Clause 2 is the substantive change and the reason clause 7 exists. The March 21, 2017 resolution had provided that the district "desires to develop an Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16 and preserve the balance of the subject property." Nine months of design work later, the site moves to the vacant land at the Niles Continuing Education site — and the supersession clause quietly voids the Section 16 siting. That single change is what made the rest of the district's land program possible: with the preschool no longer needing eight acres of Section 16, the whole 19.43-acre parcel could be sold to Mondrian Properties in March 2018, and the preschool was ultimately built at 205 Square Lake Road, the address that appears on the 2018 bid tabulations.

Clause 5 also broadens the March rule materially. The March resolution restricted revenue from "these property sales" — the specific parcels it had named. This clause restricts revenue from *any* sale of property over a two-and-a-half-year window ending June 30, 2020, which captures the Section 16 sale, the Section 1 front parcel, the Wattles Road parcel and the Boyd Street strip, all of which were still ahead.

Clause 4's $4,700,000 transfer from Capital Maintenance is the first real money committed to the project, and clause 6 completes the professional team — TMP Architecture appointed in March as architect of record, Barton Malow appointed here as construction manager of record, both firms already working on the district's bond program.

Read against what followed, this resolution is the hinge. Three months later the Board would authorize bonds without a vote of the electors and award the construction contracts; the naming resolution of December 2018 would cite the same World Class pillar language used here. But the decision that shaped everything — where the building goes, what fund holds the money, and that every land sale for the next two and a half years belongs to the preschool — is made in these seven clauses.

**Other 10.A: Board Governance Standards.** MASB's Board of Education Governance Standards are intended to help support school boards in their efforts to govern responsibly and effectively on behalf of all students. By adopting the Governance Standards, boards take an important step toward demonstrating their commitment to governing effectively on behalf of students and promoting greater self-awareness of their role.

Read as a whole, the December 2017 packet closes the year by committing the district's future. It endorses a statewide finding that Michigan does not know what educating a child costs, extends its secretaries' contract to 2021, spends $1,498,090.00 on roofs and $82,700.00 on abatement — the latter on a resolution naming the wrong company for the wrong amount, corrected four weeks later — and then, in seven clauses, decides where the preschool will be built, creates the fund that will pay for it, and assigns to that fund the proceeds of every piece of land the district sells for the next two and a half years.
